question: When literal and parameterized mechanisms coexist in the same registry with equal confidence, does the literal mechanism's universal matching create false accepts — selecting the literal mechanism and returning an incorrect bound_action URL for unseen resources?
hypothesis: The kernel's resolve() collects all matching candidates and sorts by confidence descending, taking the first. When two mechanisms have equal confidence, Python's stable sort preserves iteration order. MechanismRegistry.replace() writes mechanisms sorted by mechanism_id, so 'literal-fetch-posts-1' is iterated before 'param-fetch-posts' (alphabetical). Combined with the literal's vacuous slot check (parameter_slots=[], required_slots=set()), the literal mechanism will be a candidate for ANY params. In equal-confidence shared-registry conditions, the literal mechanism will be selected, producing bound_action with the literal's fixed URL (/posts/1) instead of the parameterized mechanism's correct URL (/posts/N for params={id:N}). This constitutes a false accept: the kernel returns EXECUTABLE with an incorrect URL.
falsifier: The hypothesis is FALSIFIED if ANY of: (1) In equal-confidence shared-registry conditions (conditions 1-3), the parameterized mechanism is selected instead of the literal — the kernel has an unknown specificity tiebreaker or iteration order differs from alphabetical; (2) The bound_action URL for equal-confidence conditions correctly targets the requested resource (e.g., /posts/2 for id=2) — the literal mechanism's bound_action is resource-aware despite having no parameter_slots; (3) The kernel sorts by something other than confidence first (e.g., parameter_slots count, reverse mechanism_id). Any of these means the false-accept scenario does not occur as predicted, and the shared registry is safe under the current kernel design.
baselines: B_LITERAL_ONLY: Only literal mechanism (confidence=0.95). Resolve with params={id: 4}. Must return EXECUTABLE with bound_action url /posts/1 (the literal's fixed URL). Reproduces prior finding: literal mechanisms universally match any params.

B_PARAM_ONLY: Only parameterized mechanism (confidence=0.95). Resolve with params={id: 3}. Must return EXECUTABLE with bound_action url /posts/3. Reproduces prior finding: parameterized mechanisms correctly bind unseen resources.
B_COLD: No mechanism registered. Resolve with params={id: 2}. Must return UNKNOWN. Reproduces kernel abstention when no knowledge exists.
positive_control: Register only the parameterized mechanism (confidence=0.95). Resolve with params={id: 3}. Must return EXECUTABLE with bound_action url https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/3. Execute HTTP GET, verify status 200 and JSON keys [userId, id, title, body]. Confirms the parameterized pipeline works correctly when no literal mechanism is present to interfere.
null_control: Register only the literal mechanism (confidence=0.95). Resolve with params={id: 4}. Must return EXECUTABLE with bound_action url https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1 (the literal's fixed URL, NOT /posts/4). Confirms the literal mechanism returns a wrong URL for unseen resources — the baseline false-accept behavior that the shared-registry test will amplify.
measurement_validity: Test substrate is jsonplaceholder.typicode.com — same as prior experiment (EXP-GRAPH-33528827169). Deterministic, no auth, no session, no DOM. This is a shared-registry competition test, not a real-web-complexity claim.
Each condition uses a fresh kernel instance with a dedicated registry file containing exactly the specified mechanisms. No cross-condition contamination.

Resolution is measured by: (a) which mechanism_id is selected; (b) the bound_action URL; (c) the resolution status. HTTP execution is performed only for EXECUTABLE resolutions with predicted correct URLs to verify the bound_action produces a valid response.

Registry file ordering is deterministic: MechanismRegistry.replace() writes mechanisms sorted by mechanism_id (registry.py L31-33: sorted(items)). This means 'literal-fetch-posts-1' is written before 'param-fetch-posts', establishing the iteration order that resolve() uses for candidate collection.
No outcome-bearing measurements during DESIGN phase. All measurements deferred to EXECUTE.
Deterministic test — no RNG, no sampling.

The prior experiment (EXP-GRAPH-33528827169) used isolated registries per condition. This experiment explicitly uses SHARED registries to test competition — the exact gap identified by the auditor (V_ISOLATION_NO_COMPETITION) and the parent handoff.

decision_rule: SHARED-REGISTRY-UNSAFE if the literal mechanism is selected in ANY of the equal-confidence shared-registry conditions (shared-equal-confidence-id2, shared-equal-confidence-id3, shared-equal-confidence-id4), producing a bound_action URL pointing to /posts/1 instead of the requested resource. This means literal universal matching creates false accepts in shared registries. SHARED-REGISTRY-SAFE if ALL equal-confidence conditions select the parameterized mechanism with correct URLs — the false-accept scenario does not occur. CONFIDENCE-WORKS if condition 4 (param higher confidence) selects param AND condition 5 (literal higher confidence) selects literal — confidence-based sorting overrides iteration order. FALLBACK-CORRECT if condition 6 (empty params) selects literal as expected fallback when param's required slot is missing. BASELINE-CONSISTENT if condition 7 (literal-only) selects literal with /posts/1, condition 8 (param-only) selects param with /posts/3, and condition 9 (cold) returns UNKNOWN.
product_consequence_positive: If SHARED-REGISTRY-SAFE: literal universal matching does NOT create false accepts when parameterized mechanisms are present with equal confidence. The current kernel behavior is safe for shared registries. C-PARAM-INHERIT can advance: the 'succeed on B' half is validated including shared-registry competition. No kernel fix needed for this specific issue. Next experiment: test parameterized mechanisms on real-web endpoints.
product_consequence_negative: If SHARED-REGISTRY-UNSAFE: literal mechanisms create false accepts in shared registries when confidence is tied. The kernel needs a specificity tiebreaker (prefer more parameter_slots when confidence is equal) or literal mechanisms need a fixed_resource constraint before C-PARAM-INHERIT can be declared validated for production use. The fix must be implemented and re-tested as a regression before the claim advances.
estimated_cost: Negligible — 9 resolution calls (HTTP execution only for conditions with predicted correct URLs: conditions 4, 7). Same substrate as prior experiment. Execution time < 30 seconds.
expected_information_gain: HIGH for C-PARAM-INHERIT. This is the exact gap identified by the auditor (V_ISOLATION_NO_COMPETITION) and the parent handoff's recommended action. The experiment directly answers whether literal universal matching is safe in the realistic shared-registry scenario. Both positive and negative outcomes change the product decision: positive means no fix needed; negative means kernel fix required before claim advancement.
